Ransomware resilience: closing the gap between endpoint security and backup

ScrollAbu Dhabi — India

7 November 2026 · 3 min read

By the Cybersecurity team at Hamdaz Technologies

In this guide

  1. Prevention is necessary, but no longer enough
  2. Why one incident reaches the whole business
  3. What a resilience layer adds
  4. Test recovery before you need it
  5. Plan the response as well as the defence
  6. A practical first step

Why endpoint security and backups alone leave UAE organisations exposed to ransomware, and the practical steps that close the gap between them.

Prevention is necessary, but no longer enough

Most UAE organisations have invested in two lines of ransomware defence. Endpoint tools (EPP, EDR or XDR) try to stop the attack on the device. Backups, ideally immutable, are the safety net if prevention fails. Both matter, and neither should be removed. The problem is what happens between them.

Modern ransomware is designed to evade endpoint detection, then go after the backups and shadow copies you would use to recover. Many attacks now steal data before they encrypt it. Halcyon, the anti-ransomware vendor, reports that 80% of ransomware attacks involve data theft before encryption. That means a clean restore does not end the incident: the data is already outside your control, and the extortion continues.

Why one incident reaches the whole business

A ransomware attack is not just an IT outage. It brings direct financial loss, possible regulatory fines, lost customer trust, reputational damage, operational disruption, data exposure and lost productivity, often all at once. The World Economic Forum’s Global Cybersecurity Outlook 2025 describes a growing cyber resilience gap, with smaller organisations prime targets and AI-powered attacks raising the pace.

For regulated sectors in the UAE, the stakes are higher still. Healthcare providers in Abu Dhabi answer to ADHICS, Dubai entities to DESC ISR, and personal data falls under the UAE PDPL. A breach that exposes data can trigger reporting duties as well as recovery work.

What a resilience layer adds

The answer is not to replace your endpoint tools or backups but to add a layer focused only on ransomware behaviour, sitting between the two. In our practice we use the Halcyon anti-ransomware platform for this. Whatever product you choose, look for these capabilities:

  • Pre-execution prevention and ransomware-specific heuristics that stop known and unknown strains before they run.
  • Behavioural modelling that detects encryption in progress and halts it.
  • Protection of backups and Volume Shadow Copies (VSS), so recovery points survive the attack.
  • Data exfiltration prevention, to reduce the risk of double extortion.
  • Key material intercept, so data can be decrypted and recovered without paying a ransom.
  • Round-the-clock monitoring by people, not just software.

Test recovery before you need it

A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a plan. Agree recovery point and recovery time objectives (RPO and RTO) with the business, then test against them. A ransomware readiness assessment should check backup isolation and immutability, restore times, high availability and disaster recovery arrangements, and whether business continuity plans still match how you operate.

Validation should be continuous, not annual. Breach and attack simulation can show whether controls still block the techniques ransomware groups use. Track a few clear measures over time: mean time to detect and respond, monitoring coverage, remediation within SLA, RPO and RTO readiness, and the trend in your risk register.

Plan the response as well as the defence

When an attack does land, speed and order matter. Decide in advance who leads, who decides on containment and who speaks to regulators and customers. A good incident response retainer covers containment, evicting the attacker, digital forensics and support with regulatory reporting. Pair it with 24/7 managed detection and response, so someone is watching when attacks start, which is often outside office hours.

Keep decision authority with your own team. A managed service should act within agreed escalation rules, report monthly and review risk and the roadmap with you each quarter.

A practical first step

Start by finding out where your gaps are. Our Cyber Resilience Assessment runs from scope and kick-off, through discovery and technical review, to findings and a roadmap. It sets your current posture against NIST CSF 2.0 and ISO 27001, includes a ransomware readiness view, and delivers a prioritised risk register, quick wins, a 12-month roadmap and a board-ready summary. As a cybersecurity company in Abu Dhabi, Hamdaz can then help you design, implement and operate the controls, from the data centre to the end user.

If you already run endpoint protection and immutable backup, you are not starting from scratch. The work is to connect them: add the missing layer, prove recovery against agreed RPO and RTO, and make sure someone is watching around the clock. That is what turns a set of separate tools into resilience the business can rely on.
